claims.text: A chromosome is one DNA molecule combined with histone proteins; the DNA is wound around the histones and coiled further, which packs a molecule far longer than the nucleus into a compact structure that can be moved when the cell divides.

claims.text: Mitosis is the division of a nucleus to give two nuclei with the same number and kind of chromosomes as the parent nucleus; the daughter nuclei are genetically identical because the DNA is replicated first and one of the two sister chromatids of each chromosome is passed to each nucleus.

claims.text: Because mitosis gives genetically identical cells, it is the process behind growth by increase in cell number, replacement of cells that are lost or worn out, repair of damaged tissue and asexual reproduction, in which offspring are genetically identical to the parent.

claims.text: In a root tip most cells are in interphase, with a nucleus that is intact and chromosomes not visible as separate structures; the stages of mitosis are recognised by what the chromosomes are doing: condensed and visible in prophase, lined up across the equator in metaphase, separated into two groups moving to opposite poles in anaphase, and decondensing at the poles in telophase.

claims.text: The mitotic cell cycle is interphase, then mitosis, then cytokinesis, after which the two daughter cells begin interphase again; interphase has three phases in order: G1, S and G2.

claims.text: In G1 the cell grows and makes proteins and organelles; in S phase the DNA is replicated, so each chromosome becomes two sister chromatids; in G2 the cell grows further and prepares for mitosis; cytokinesis then divides the cytoplasm to give two cells.

claims.text: Interphase is usually the longest part of the cycle and mitosis a short part, so in a sample of dividing tissue most cells are in interphase; the time spent in a stage is estimated as the fraction of cells in that stage multiplied by the length of the cycle, provided the cells are not dividing in step with one another.
